Reading / source: Howard Zinn, A People's History (selected chapter) + primary sources + a competing mainstream historical account
Learning outcome: Separate event, source, selection, framing and inference; detect omitted actors and asymmetric evidence.
Required analysis: Build a claim ledger for one consequential technology/history claim: exact claim, primary evidence, competing interpretation, uncertainty.
Changed artifact: Rewrite one paragraph of your capstone history/context section after source triangulation.
Oral-defense prompt: Why did you select these sources, and what source would most threaten your preferred narrative?
Pass criterion: Pass if the final narrative contains at least one material revision caused by contrary evidence.
Access/source: Proprietary book; use library. Pairing is mandatory.

Reading / source: Ibram X. Kendi, How to Be an Antiracist (selected argument) + Sasha Costanza-Chock, Design Justice (open) + empirical subgroup evidence relevant to your domain
Learning outcome: Translate normative claims into explicit objectives, mechanisms, distributions of benefit/harm and testable questions.
Required analysis: Audit your capstone objective: who defines success, whose errors count, subgroup failure, recourse and distributional effects.
Changed artifact: Add a distributional/recourse section to your system specification or evaluation plan.
Oral-defense prompt: Can two reasonable moral objectives imply different engineering designs even with identical facts?
Pass criterion: Pass if the technical objective/evaluation changes; agreement with any author is not required.

Injection point: Political thought, incentives and institutional control
Reading / source: Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Political Thought (reference) + The Logic of Political Survival + Ostrom, Governing the Commons + Hirschman, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
Learning outcome: Model authority, selector/coalition incentives, commons, exit, voice, ownership and institutional failure.
Required analysis: Create power map: decision rights, vetoes, funding, ownership, users, affected non-users, regulators, operators, maintainers and appeal routes.
Changed artifact: Redesign one governance mechanism for your capstone based on the power map.
Oral-defense prompt: Who can make the system continue operating after the evidence says stop?
Pass criterion: Pass if at least one incentive conflict produces a changed control/ownership/oversight design.

Injection point: Platforms, media, attention and organizational incentives
Reading / source: Jaron Lanier, Ten Arguments... + Sarah Wynn-Williams, Careless People + empirical research on your platform/attention hypothesis
Learning outcome: Distinguish memoir/polemic from empirical evidence; map product metrics to organizational incentives and externalities.
Required analysis: Turn three claims from the readings into measurable hypotheses; seek confirming and disconfirming evidence.
Changed artifact: If your capstone has users/engagement/agents, add anti-Goodhart metrics and attention/manipulation abuse tests.
Oral-defense prompt: What behavior would your business/model metric reward that your stated mission condemns?
Pass criterion: Pass if rhetoric is converted into falsifiable claims and at least one hypothesis is weakened or revised.
Access/source: Proprietary books; do not treat memoir as complete causal record.

Injection point: Violence, bystanders and normalization of deviance
Reading / source: Ervin Staub, The Roots of Evil / Overcoming Evil + Diane Vaughan, The Challenger Launch Decision + Nancy Leveson
Learning outcome: Understand escalation, bystander action, normalization, organizational drift and system-level accident causation.
Required analysis: Reconstruct a real incident as an escalation/control-structure timeline rather than a single-root-cause story.
Changed artifact: Add leading indicators, dissent/stop-work channels and drift monitoring to capstone operations.
Oral-defense prompt: What weak signal will your organization normalize after it has succeeded ten times?
Pass criterion: Pass if incident analysis changes monitoring, authority or shutdown design.

Injection point: Wicked problems and limits of optimizer metaphors
Reading / source: Rittel & Webber, Dilemmas in a General Theory of Planning + selected wicked-problem literature
Learning outcome: Recognize problems with contested formulations, plural values, one-shot consequences and changing requirements.
Required analysis: Write three incompatible formulations of the same frontier deployment and show how each changes the optimum.
Changed artifact: Replace a single optimum with reversible portfolio, monitoring triggers, recourse and reformulation schedule.
Oral-defense prompt: What if solving your formulation makes the underlying social problem worse?
Pass criterion: Pass if learner explicitly identifies where quantitative optimization remains valid and where it does not decide the objective.

Injection point: Nonviolent communication, difficult conversations and design conflict
Reading / source: CNVC NVC framework + Difficult Conversations + Conscious Leadership resources
Learning outcome: Separate observation from interpretation, surface interests/needs, handle identity threat, and preserve adversarial technical disagreement.
Required analysis: Run a recorded design review with two assigned roles whose incentives conflict; first use adversarial bargaining, then structured listening/request methods.
Changed artifact: Write decision record: disagreements, evidence, unresolved interests, concessions and test that can decide technical dispute.
Oral-defense prompt: What conflict is about facts, what is about values, and what is about status/identity/power?
Pass criterion: Pass if the team reaches clearer disagreement or a better experiment—not necessarily consensus.

Injection point: Capital allocation, unit economics and real options
Reading / source: Wave-1/2 economics + project finance/decision analysis; use current costs from public sources relevant to your track
Learning outcome: Translate technical performance into cost, capital intensity, learning curve, option value and staged investment.
Required analysis: Build bottom-up cost model and identify the technical parameter with greatest economic elasticity.
Changed artifact: Design a staged financing/research plan where each tranche buys information and preserves abandonment option.
Oral-defense prompt: Which technical breakthrough would *not* make the project economically deployable?
Pass criterion: Pass if a technical improvement is rejected because another bottleneck dominates total value.
Access/source: Use current public cost sources; document date and scenario.

Injection point: Law, standards, regulation and permission to operate
Learning outcome: Distinguish legal minimum, industry standard, safety case, ethical commitment and internal policy.
Required analysis: Build a compliance/standards matrix for capstone: requirement, authority, evidence, owner, verification and update trigger.
Changed artifact: Identify one design decision that becomes different because of a standard/regulatory obligation.
Oral-defense prompt: Where is compliance necessary but insufficient for safety or legitimacy?
Pass criterion: Pass if primary authority is cited and requirements are traceable to verification evidence.
Access/source: Use current primary/official sources for chosen domain.

Reading / source: Your track's primary paper + reproducibility/open-science guidance
Learning outcome: Write claims with evidence tiers; package code/data/configuration; report null/negative/adversarial results.
Required analysis: Reproduce your capstone from clean environment; another person follows README without oral help.
Changed artifact: Create release package: paper, data provenance, environment, tests, limitations, negative-results appendix.
Oral-defense prompt: What claim in your abstract is least supported by the artifacts?
Pass criterion: Pass if an independent person can reproduce the central figure/result and identify unsupported claims.

Injection point: Design the lab/company/team that can keep learning
Reading / source: Ostrom/Hirschman/Leveson/Edmondson-style organizational learning + your own operating doctrine
Learning outcome: Design decision rights, dissent, review, incentives, documentation, hiring and knowledge retention.
Required analysis: Write a 2-page lab/company constitution: mission, non-goals, decision rights, stop-work authority, review cadence, evidence standards, conflict process.
Changed artifact: Run a tabletop scenario: founder/PI wants to ship; safety lead objects; funder deadline looms; data are ambiguous.
Oral-defense prompt: What organizational rule remains good when you personally are no longer in charge?
Pass criterion: Pass if structure protects dissent and evidence against both bureaucracy and charismatic override.
Access/source: Synthesis from prior sources; explicitly marked as design proposal.

Injection point: Final public defense and 12-month frontier program
Reading / source: All prior work; no new reading
Learning outcome: Integrate technical, empirical, economic, institutional and human evidence into a bounded thesis and action program.
Required analysis: From blank page: state problem, physical/causal model, evidence, uncertainty, bottleneck, stakeholders/power, risks, economics and next experiment.
Changed artifact: Deliver public dossier + 30-minute talk + 60-minute adversarial oral defense + prioritized 12-month roadmap with kill/pivot criteria.
Oral-defense prompt: What is the strongest argument that you should *not* pursue this program?
Pass criterion: Final pass requires technically credible work, explicit uncertainty, reproducibility, moral/political self-critique and a falsifiable next move.
